Ben and database reviewer50-database.tex · 4I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb), a curated literature resource for studying sensory feedback in locomotion and posture. It links findings from animal and human studies to afferent classes, sensory afferent pathways, and computational models. Researchers can use these records to compare individual feedback connections or whole neural circuits before implementing a neuromechanical model. This work forms part of the AARL's NeuroNex Communication, Coordination, and Control in Nervous Systems (C3NS) effort.Why create SADb?

Names the nerve, response, preparation, and modeling choice that make a source-linked collection necessary.

Current sourceChoosing a sensory connection for a locomotor controller requires more than the name of a receptor. A researcher needs to know which nerve was stimulated, which motor neurons responded, and whether the animal was at rest or moving. Those details are scattered across studies that used different species, preparations, and tasks. I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) to keep a proposed feedback pathway linked to the experiment that supports it. The collection also links to computational models so that a researcher can compare an experimental finding with the assumptions used to represent it. This work forms part of the AARL's NeuroNex Communication, Coordination, and Control in Nervous Systems (C3NS) effort.

Primary experiment and independent reader50-database.tex · 64For example, a researcher may ask whether type Ia feedback excites the muscle from which it originates or inhibits its antagonist. SADb contains separate pathway records for ``Ia monosynaptic excitation'' and ``Ia inhibitory.'' These describe complementary connections: direct excitation of the agonist motor pool and inhibition of an antagonist through an inhibitory interneuron. The researcher can inspect the linked studies and model records to compare their target muscles, intervening neurons, and task conditions before choosing how to implement the sensory afferent pathways. The afferent class alone does not specify the sign of every connection.\parWhat can a modeler take from the experiment?

The same group I nerve stimulus inhibited the synergist motor pool at rest and excited it during extension in midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion. A signed diagram conveys the net response without assigning unmeasured interneurons or gains.

Current sourceIn decerebrate cats at rest, stimulating the plantaris nerve at group~I strength inhibited medial gastrocnemius motor neurons. With the same stimulus during extension in midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion, the recorded response was excitatory. In this preparation the neural rhythm was present while the animal was immobilized. Nerve stimulation recruited group~I fibers and did not isolate Ib fibers.

Defense-folder audit60-sns.tex · 172The search scripts bound the parameters, tie corresponding left and right values when symmetry is intended, and use tree-structured Parzen estimation to select candidates from earlier scores. They save the parameters, components of the score, and reason each trial ended. A selected candidate is rerun in a fresh process before any intervention.What did the fitting tool vary?

TPE proposes rhythm and timing parameters. Bounded least squares fits pattern-formation to motor-neuron weights in s3k and syn6.

Current sourceFor rhythm and sensory timing, the search scripts use tree-structured Parzen estimation to propose new parameter sets from earlier scores. For the s3k and syn6 controllers, a separate bounded least-squares fit adjusts the connections from pattern-formation channels to motor neurons to match the reference muscle recruitment. Corresponding weights are tied across sides when the fit calls for symmetry. The physical test then loads the saved settings, records the components of its score and the reason the trial ended, and repeats a selected trial in a fresh process before an intervention.

Ben and curation evaluation70-overall.tex · 67The monthly literature watch supplies candidates for manual curation (Section~\ref{sec:sadb_methods}). For a pathway such as extensor group~I excitation, the most useful addition to a record would be a direct link from each reported sign to its preparation, stimulus, and phase. A reader could then distinguish a measured reversal from an assumption in a computational model before following their citation links. The Bubble map already identifies citation communities by color. Grouping their papers spatially would provide a second way to locate related studies \citep{bolen_using_2024}.What has to change for assisted classification to be viable?

Propose source-grounded labels, an independent curation comparison, and a human decision. The Chomsky, Roberts, and Watumull guest essay is an argument about explanation. The empirical test uses the project's screening experience.

Current sourceFuture researchers can revisit large language models for classification as the tools improve. In our earlier evaluation, finding related papers was more successful than assigning them to the right categories \citep{bolen_using_2024}. A model could propose a pathway label and identify the passage that supports it. A researcher would read the experiment and approve, correct, or reject the label before it enters SADb. \citet{chomsky_false_promise_2023} distinguish predicting plausible text from explaining why a conclusion follows. In the McCrea example, the words \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} alone do not tell a curator which fibers were stimulated. Comparing suggested labels with independently curated records, and measuring the time required to check them, would show whether newer models help with that work.

Ben, advisor comment, and independent reader60-sns.tex · 4I developed the tools in this chapter to couple neural controllers to Gait2392, a human musculoskeletal model, and to mechanical models based on the computer-aided design (CAD) of our bipedal robot. Slow simulation and hand tuning in an earlier course project with Connor Morrow made it difficult to repeat the same experiment after changing the controller or the mechanical model. A scripted version of the walker in the MuJoCo physics engine made automatic tuning possible. The subsequent experiments use the human model, a robot counterpart with relocated muscle paths, and a model built from the lab robot's own geometry. I developed Simulink blocks and a graphical interface for building nonspiking circuits. A simulated knee reflex tests whether a sensory signal passes through a motor neuron and muscle to produce joint motion. The final experiments use scripts to tune controllers, test whether the feet alternate under load, and measure how much a faster neural calculation saves over a complete trial.What questions required new tools and a robot-specific model?

The lab needed systematic controller tuning and models that could return feedback from the motion produced by the robot's own muscle paths and joints. Changing one connection or attachment and repeating the trial reveals its effect on muscle force and leg motion.

Current sourceThis chapter presents the tools I developed to test neural controllers on a human musculoskeletal model and on models of our bipedal robot. The lab's existing software made it impractical to search systematically for controller settings. The human model provided a reference for movement, but testing the robot required a model that represented where its artificial muscles pulled on the joints and how the resulting motion fed back to the controller. I built tools to construct circuits graphically, connect controllers to these mechanical models, and automate tuning. Researchers can now change a sensory connection or move an artificial muscle attachment in simulation, repeat the trial under the same conditions, and trace the effect on muscle force and leg motion.

Ben, advisor comment, and independent reader60-sns.tex · 8I built my first neuromechanical model in AnimatLab, a graphical program in which a neural circuit can activate muscles and receive sensory signals from the moving body \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. For the course project, Morrow and I connected the circuit of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} to the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} and adjusted neural currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand. The circuit supplied a common rhythm to both legs, and opposing muscles pulled on each limb. There is a passive toe joint. The legs made stepping-like movements while the model was suspended in air. When we lowered it to the ground and removed the support, the model fell over (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Each parameter change required another slow run, making a systematic search impractical.Which earlier experiment exposed the limitation?

Morrow and Bolen tested the published Deng circuit on the Li biped. The legs made stepping-like movements in suspension, the model fell when support was removed, and each parameter change cost another slow run. This is the reader's first account of the course project.

Current sourceIn a course project, Connor Morrow and I tested whether the neural circuit of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} could coordinate the legs of the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017}. We connected the circuit and body in AnimatLab, a graphical program for linking neurons, muscles, and sensory feedback \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}, and adjusted neural currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand. The circuit supplied a common rhythm to both legs, and opposing muscles pulled on each limb. There is a passive toe joint. The legs made stepping-like movements while the model was suspended in air. When we lowered it to the ground and removed the support, the model fell over (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Each parameter change required another slow run.

Earlier reviewAuthor directions and independent findingsBen · first person60-sns.tex · Chapter 6, opening, §6.1, and conclusion
Earlier wording or marked passage I developed the tools in this chapter to couple neural controllers to mechanical models derived from Gait2392, a human musculoskeletal model, and from the computer-aided design (CAD) geometry of our bipedal robot. Our first simulated walker ran slowly, and we tuned its neural parameters by hand. I begin with that walker, then show how I used the MuJoCo physics engine to test the same controller repeatedly and wrote scripts to automate the search for controller settings. I then describe how I expanded the neural controllers on Gait2392, relocated muscle paths for pneumatic actuators in its robot counterpart, and coupled a controller to the lab robot’s CAD model. Finally, I describe the graphical tools I built to edit large neural circuits and use a simulated knee reflex to verify that a sensory pulse recruits the extensor motor neuron, increases muscle force, and extends the knee.
Change and rationale Credit concrete contributions, identify collaborative work, and let the tool or experiment state its behavior.

Earlier reviewAuthor directions and independent findingsBen · preserve Introduction10-introduction.tex · Ch. 1, Motivation, final paragraph
Earlier wording or marked passage The sensory pathways documented in the database suggest how the nervous system uses feedback from the legs to coordinate movement. To simulate what those pathways contribute, it is possible to combine a neural circuit model with the mechanical model of the body it controls. The circuit activates muscles, their forces move the joints, and the resulting changes in muscle stretch and load feed back to the circuit and shape its next commands. The robot’s artificial muscles differ from human muscles in how much force they produce and where they pull on the skeleton. A circuit that coordinates the legs of the human model will therefore produce a different movement in the robot model, and that movement will change the sensory feedback the circuit receives. To measure the effect of the mechanics, I wanted to repeat the same experiment on both models with the controller held fixed. I also wanted to test changes to the controller while keeping the mechanical model fixed. Our first neuromechanical model ran slowly, and we tuned its controller by hand, making a series of these comparisons impractical. I therefore developed tools to build circuits graphically, automate their tuning, and run those comparisons on a human musculoskeletal model and on models built from our robot's mechanical design (Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}). With human movement as a reference, the new system can simulate how changing a sensory connection or moving an artificial muscle attachment affects a mechanical model's coordination.
Change and rationale The local copy reproduces “combine … with” and the advisor’s ending verbatim.

Earlier wording or marked passage A researcher can reproduce the knee experiment with \path{run_transient.m} and the archived \texttt{KneeReflexDemo} model. The driver runs the settled knee twice and adds a \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{30}{\milli\second} pulse to the extensor Ia current in one run. The pulse recruited the extensor MN. The flexor was already inactive, so the rise in extensor force accounted for the initial extension (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_reflex_current}). The stimulated knee extended \ang{1.09} relative to the control, peaked \qty{111}{\milli\second} after pulse onset, and met the angle and speed recovery criteria \qty{6.355}{\second} after onset. Broader MN and Ia synaptic operating ranges allowed the model to settle before the pulse. The original narrow ranges produced sustained oscillation. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} gives the MATLAB command and the fields to inspect in the saved summary.

Earlier wording or marked passage I adapted the W2L circuit to the Gait2392 human model. In this variant, W2Lvar, one pair of pattern-forming channels coordinates the hip muscles on each side and another coordinates the knee and ankle muscles. The full circuit had 888 neurons and 7,868 connected neuron pairs. To change knee extensor recruitment, it is necessary to find the inputs to its motor pool, the group of motor neurons that drives the muscle, and inspect their synapses. I built graphical tools that let me work on that part of the circuit by function. Scripts assemble repeated connections and run parameter trials. Table~\ref{tab:sns_capability} gives the entry points for the mechanical, neural, and fitting tools.

I set the intrinsic period to approximately twice the target locomotor period, tuned the rhythm so that it synchronized with the expected sensory input, fitted feedforward motor recruitment, and refined the pattern with sensory feedback. Earlier wording or marked passage MyoConverter translates OpenSim muscle paths and joint geometry into a model that runs in MuJoCo \citep{caggiano_myosuite_2022,wang_myosim_2022}. I applied it to the human reference, \path{gait2392_simbody.osim}, and drove the muscles with neural controllers. Graded neurons transmit signals that vary continuously with membrane voltage. Spiking neurons transmit discrete events when their voltage reaches a threshold. Before fitting a circuit, I restored missing maximum-force scales from the OpenSim source and checked that a pull on each tested muscle moved the joint in the intended direction. The model retains 92 actuator entries, including six small hip rotators that remain disabled, and the OpenSim convention of negative knee flexion. Earlier reviewFirst-use review (27)Ben · FIRST-0160-sns.tex, line 9 · AnimatLab
Earlier wording or anchor In AnimatLab, Morrow and I tuned our first walker by changing currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand and running the model again. Each motor neuron recruits a muscle, the muscle pulls on the limb, and sensory signals from the moving limb return to the circuit. A change in any part of that loop can alter the next step. Runs with the older solver were slow enough to make hand tuning impractical for a large parameter search. I wanted to change the controller or the leg geometry, repeat the same test, and identify where the response changed.
Proposed wording or action Morrow and I built our first simulated walker in AnimatLab, a graphical program that couples a neural circuit to a moving body \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. To tune the walker, we changed currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand and ran it again. Each motor neuron recruits a muscle, the muscle pulls on the limb, and sensory signals from the moving limb return to the circuit. A change in any part of that loop can alter the next step. Runs with the older solver were slow enough to make hand tuning impractical for a large parameter search. I wanted to change the controller or the leg geometry, repeat the same test, and identify where the response changed.
Reason and evidence The opening used AnimatLab as a familiar program name.
Disposition on that date The opening now identifies graphical software coupling a neural circuit to a moving body and describes the variables Morrow and Bolen adjusted. Applied locally, 3/4.		As recorded on the review date
Earlier reviewFirst-use review (27)Independent dissertation reader · FIRST-0260-sns.tex, line 11 · Li–Deng and CPG
Earlier wording or anchor For a course project in neuromechanical modeling, Morrow and I coupled the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} to the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. A shared rhythm generator (RG) drove pattern-formation (PF) pathways and motor neurons (MNs) on both sides. Antagonist Hill-type muscles acted on the thighs, shanks, and feet. I added a passive toe joint. Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Its legs cycled in suspension and the model tipped when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}).
Proposed wording or action For a course project in neuromechanical modeling, Morrow and I coupled the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} to the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019}, a neural circuit that produces rhythmic motor commands. In this Li--Deng walker, a shared rhythm generator (RG) set the period of the cycle. Pattern-formation (PF) pathways determined when motor neurons (MNs) recruited each muscle group. Opposing Hill-type muscle models used contractile and elastic elements to pull on the thighs, shanks, and feet. I added a passive toe joint. Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Its legs cycled in suspension and the model tipped when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}).
Reason and evidence The study names, RG, and PF identified a source without explaining which parts produced the rhythm or timed the muscles.
Disposition on that date Li supplied the sagittal-plane biped. Deng supplied the two-level circuit. RG sets its period and PF times motor recruitment. The chapter introduces both before Figure 6.1. Applied locally, 3/4.		As recorded on the review date
Earlier reviewFirst-use review (27)Ben · FIRST-0360-sns.tex, line 31 · MuJoCo and SNS-Toolbox
Earlier wording or anchor I used MuJoCo to calculate movement and contact and SNS-Toolbox to evaluate the synthetic nervous system (SNS) \citep{todorov_mujoco_2012,nourse_sns_2023}. I connected the two in scripts so that I could save a controller, change one parameter or pathway, and repeat a trial under the same mechanical conditions. In a later walker model, W2L, the bilateral circuits received heel and toe contact signals from the simulated feet during supported treadmill stepping. I could turn off selected pathways and measure whether the two feet still alternated under load.
Proposed wording or action MuJoCo (Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact) is the physics engine I used to calculate joint motion and ground contact forces \citep{todorov_mujoco_2012}. I ran the controller in SNS-Toolbox, a Python library for simulating the neurons and synapses of a synthetic nervous system (SNS) \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Connecting the two programs let me change a pathway and repeat a trial under the same mechanical conditions.
Reason and evidence The reader had to infer whether MuJoCo and SNS-Toolbox were competing simulators or separate parts of the test.
Disposition on that date The physics engine calculates motion and contact. The Python library simulates the neurons and synapses coupled to it. Applied locally, 3/4.		As recorded on the review date
Earlier reviewFirst-use review (27)Ben, earlier directive U23 · FIRST-0460-sns.tex, line 33 · Walker Two-Layer
Earlier wording or anchor I used MuJoCo to calculate movement and contact and SNS-Toolbox to evaluate the synthetic nervous system (SNS) \citep{todorov_mujoco_2012,nourse_sns_2023}. I connected the two in scripts so that I could save a controller, change one parameter or pathway, and repeat a trial under the same mechanical conditions. In a later walker model, W2L, the bilateral circuits received heel and toe contact signals from the simulated feet during supported treadmill stepping. I could turn off selected pathways and measure whether the two feet still alternated under load.
Proposed wording or action I developed the Walker Two-Layer (W2L) controller from the Li--Deng walker. I gave each leg its own rhythm generator, linked the two sides, and fed heel and toe contact signals from the simulated feet back to the circuit. During supported stepping on level ground, I could turn off selected pathways and measure whether the feet still alternated under load.
Reason and evidence The earlier chapter wrote “In a later walker model, W2L” and had lost an already documented author correction.
Disposition on that date The first named appearance spells out Walker Two-Layer. The shared rhythm generator becomes one per leg. The simulated heels and toes feed contact information back to the circuit. Applied locally, 3/4. One author-prompted deduction of −2 for the recurring issue.		As recorded on the review date

Earlier reviewFirst-use review (27)Independent technical reader · FIRST-0960-sns.tex, line 67 · MyoConverter and neural signals
Earlier wording or anchor I used MyoConverter \citep{wang_myosim_2022} to convert the human reference, \path{gait2392_simbody.osim}, then drove its biological-muscle actuators in MuJoCo with a neural controller. Before fitting a circuit, I restored missing maximum-force scales from the OpenSim source and checked that a pull on each tested muscle moved the joint in the intended direction. The model retains 92 actuator entries, including six small hip rotators that remain disabled, and the OpenSim convention of negative knee flexion. I moved each joint through its range to check changes in moment arm at moving points and wrap surfaces, and checked that ground forces arose from foot contact (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_conversion_repairs}).
Proposed wording or action MyoConverter translates OpenSim muscle paths and joint geometry into a model that runs in MuJoCo \citep{caggiano_myosuite_2022,wang_myosim_2022}. I applied it to the human reference, \path{gait2392_simbody.osim}, and drove the muscles with neural controllers. Graded neurons transmit signals that vary continuously with membrane voltage. Spiking neurons transmit discrete events when their voltage reaches a threshold. Before fitting a circuit, I restored missing maximum-force scales from the OpenSim source and checked that a pull on each tested muscle moved the joint in the intended direction. The model retains 92 actuator entries, including six small hip rotators that remain disabled, and the OpenSim convention of negative knee flexion. I moved each joint through its range to check changes in moment arm at moving points and wrap surfaces, and checked that ground forces arose from foot contact (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_conversion_repairs}).
Reason and evidence Converter credit and the graded and spiking circuits needed an operating description.
Disposition on that date The converter translates geometry and paths. Graded neurons carry a continuously varying signal. Spiking neurons emit events at threshold. Applied locally, 3/4.		As recorded on the review date
Earlier reviewFirst-use review (27)Independent technical reader · FIRST-1060-sns.tex, line 69 · Static optimization
Earlier wording or anchor At matched poses and OpenSim static-optimization activations, eight of twelve sampled muscles gave force-prediction $R^2$ values of 0.88--0.98 and mean forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of the reference (Table~\ref{tab:force-r2}). Rectus femoris and biceps femoris short head had negative $R^2$. For those muscles, the mean reference force predicted the sampled force better than the converted model did. This comparison prescribed a pose and activation for each frame. Movement velocity and tendon dynamics were outside its scope.
Proposed wording or action For the force check, I prescribed the activations from OpenSim static optimization, which estimates how muscles share the load at each reference pose \citep{opensim_static_optimization_docs}. With pose and activation matched, eight of twelve sampled muscles gave force-prediction $R^2$ values of 0.88--0.98 and mean forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of the reference (Table~\ref{tab:force-r2}). Rectus femoris and biceps femoris short head had negative $R^2$. For those muscles, the mean reference force predicted the sampled force better than the converted model did. This comparison prescribed a pose and activation for each frame. Movement velocity and tendon dynamics were outside its scope.
Reason and evidence The source of the reference activations was named before the reader knew what it estimated.
Disposition on that date The force comparison now identifies how static optimization estimates muscle load sharing at individual poses. Its citation is shared with Appendix D. Applied locally, 3/4.		As recorded on the review date

Earlier reviewFirst-use review (27)Ben and independent readers · FIRST-1260-sns.tex, line 87 · W2Lvar and motor pools
Earlier wording or anchor The full W2Lvar controller for the Gait2392 human model had 888 neurons and 7,868 connected neuron pairs. To change how a knee extensor is recruited, I need to identify the neurons that feed its motor pool and inspect their synaptic parameters. I built graphical tools that let me work on that part of the circuit by function. Scripts assemble repeated connections and run parameter trials. Table~\ref{tab:sns_capability} gives the entry points for the mechanical, neural, and fitting tools.
Proposed wording or action I adapted the W2L circuit to the Gait2392 human model. In this variant, W2Lvar, one pair of pattern-forming channels coordinates the hip muscles on each side and another coordinates the knee and ankle muscles. The full circuit had 888 neurons and 7,868 connected neuron pairs. To change knee extensor recruitment, I need to find the inputs to its motor pool, the group of motor neurons that drives the muscle, and inspect their synapses. I built graphical tools that let me work on that part of the circuit by function. Scripts assemble repeated connections and run parameter trials. Table~\ref{tab:sns_capability} gives the entry points for the mechanical, neural, and fitting tools.
Reason and evidence A code-like name and topology counts did not tell the reader which body or muscle organization had changed.
Disposition on that date Bolen adapted W2L to Gait2392. Each leg has one pair of hip pattern channels and another for knee and ankle. The same paragraph defines the motor pool the researcher inspects. Applied locally, 3/4.		As recorded on the review date

Earlier reviewChapter 6 sequence (16)Ben · Opening60-sns.tex, line 9
Earlier wording or anchor A neuromechanical simulation couples a neural controller to a mechanical model of the body it controls. Motor-neuron activity recruits actuators, the resulting forces move or load the joints, and sensory pathways carry measurements of that response back to the controller. I wanted to transfer a locomotor circuit from one model of the legs to another. A circuit that alternates the legs in suspension must also coordinate muscle force with foot contact if the model is to support weight. I developed tools to inspect that loop one connection at a time and to repeat a mechanical test after changing a connection. The starting point was a controller-development project in AnimatLab. Changes in muscle attachment, joint motion, and inertia alter the movement produced by a given motor command. The same motion can also stretch different muscles in two models and return a different pattern of sensory activity. These effects tie the choice of controller to the body on which it is tested.
Proposed wording or action In AnimatLab, Morrow and I tuned our first walker by changing currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand and running the model again. Each motor neuron recruits a muscle, the muscle pulls on the limb, and sensory signals from the moving limb return to the circuit. A change in any part of that loop can alter the next step. Runs with the older solver were slow enough to make hand tuning impractical for a large parameter search. I wanted to change the controller or the leg geometry, repeat the same test, and identify where the response changed.
Reason and evidence The old opening defined neuromechanics before readers knew why the AnimatLab workflow had to change.
Disposition on that date The first paragraph names the slow trial and the changes made by hand. Section 6.5 answers it with bounded searches and replay. No paired AnimatLab benchmark was recorded. Locally verified, 3/4. Prior assistant draft, -2 from Ben’s feedback.		As recorded on the review date

Earlier reviewChapter 6 sequence (16)Ben and both independent readers · Retest after CAD60-sns.tex, line 141
Earlier wording or anchor I used two routes to prepare the mechanics. For imported musculoskeletal models, I converted OpenSim geometry and muscle paths with MyoConverter and checked the result in MuJoCo. For CAD assemblies, I used joint frames, inertial properties, and attachments to assemble mechanisms for Simscape Multibody or, separately, MuJoCo. A researcher can also run a Simulink controller against existing MuJoCo mechanics through the runtime bridge. That route exchanges commands and measurements at each update and requires an executable MuJoCo model. I placed the CAD assembly in its anatomical frame ($x$ anterior, $y$ superior, and $z$ right) using a reference datum, assigned link masses and inertias, and retained the four-bar knee constraints. Actuator tension times a route's signed moment arm gives its joint torque. By virtual work, the moment arm is the negative derivative of route length with respect to joint angle, including the motion of attachment and via points. I checked this derivative by perturbing the angle with the same points active and recorded switches of conditional points separately.
Proposed wording or action Figure~\ref{fig:sns_design_fit_workflow}A follows two connections in the saved left-leg W2L circuit. One PF neuron excites the extensor motor pool and the other excites the flexor pool. Moving an attachment in CAD can change its moment arm. In a model with length feedback, it can also change the stretch signal returned to the circuit. To test such a revision, I would update the attachment and its actuator and sensor mapping, then run both models with the same saved circuit, external drive, and load. Comparing their actuator forces and joint angles would show how the change affected the closed-loop response.
Reason and evidence “Repeat the same controller input” could imply clamped sensory feedback or a completed matched CAD experiment.
Disposition on that date The proposed test holds circuit, external drive, and load fixed, recomputes feedback from each body, and compares force and angle. Stretch applies in models with length feedback. Locally verified, 3/4.		As recorded on the review date

Earlier wording or anchor I adapted the four calibration operations presented by \citet{hunt_inrc_2019}. I set the intrinsic period to approximately twice the target locomotor period, tuned entrainment under expected afferent input, fitted feedforward motor recruitment, and refined the pattern with sensory feedback. The recruitment targets came from inverse mechanics applied to reference motion. Agreement with those targets measures how well the network reproduces the estimated activation pattern. For repeated searches I used bounded parameters, tied left and right homologues where symmetry was intended, and used tree-structured Parzen estimation to select candidates. The scripts save parameters, objective components, and the termination condition. A promising candidate is rerun in a fresh process with its fitted parameters before an intervention is introduced.

Earlier wording or anchor Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero angular velocity. To determine when that capacity can do work, I would measure knee torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$ on the same time base and about the same signed axis. Their pr… Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero angular velocity. To determine when that capacity can do work, I would measure knee torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$ on the same time base and about the same signed axis. Their product $P=\tau\omega$, in watts, is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the knee to the external load. Positive power indicates energy delivery and negative power indicates absorption. Its timing and magnitude distinguish a knee that supplies energy during extension from one that resists motion to absorb a landing load. A biomechanist can compare these phases with joint-power profiles, and a robot designer can size the actuator for both propulsion and controlled deceleration. A dynamometer on the test stand could drive flexion and extension at prescribed speeds or impose a resisting torque while the BPA moves the knee. An encoder and a joint-axis torque transducer would supply synchronized velocity and torque. Recording actuator pressure and calibrating fixture inertia, friction, and loading-connection compliance would help distinguish pneumatic delay and load--unload hysteresis from losses in the rig.

Matching record by record on DOI and normalized title showed that t… The author's personal Zotero collection held 538 items, the AARL group library's Biology subtree held 911 items across 27 collections, and the Airtable base held 99 papers. Matching record by record on DOI and normalized title showed that the personal collection was essentially a subset of the group library (all 483 personal DOIs present) and that the Airtable base was a small curated subset rather than a mirror: 95 of its 99 papers resolved to records in the group library's Biology subtree, while 443 personal items had never been entered at all. The gap was imported in verified batches, with every written record re-read and checked after writing, bringing the Papers table to 532 records. The corpus then kept growing while curation caught up: citation mining in the style of Research Rabbit contributed a Crossref-verified digest of recent papers, newly saved references flowed in from the laboratory's Zotero libraries, and a bulk pass imported 372 papers auto-classified from the laboratory's staged collection of PDFs.

Earlier wording or anchor Two definitions cover most of the neuroscience vocabulary used below. First, the locomotor controller is a two-level central pattern generator: a rhythm generator sets the timing of the step cycle, and a pattern-formation layer shapes that … Two definitions cover most of the neuroscience vocabulary used below. First, the locomotor controller is a two-level central pattern generator: a rhythm generator sets the timing of the step cycle, and a pattern-formation layer shapes that timing into phase-appropriate activation of antagonist muscle groups \citep{rybak_modelling_2006}. Each leg's rhythm generator is a pair of mutually inhibiting antagonist populations, one extensor and one flexor, so that only one is strongly active at a time. Second, in the non-spiking (graded) formulation used for most of this work, each neuron is electrically a nonlinear RC circuit: synaptic current charges a membrane capacitance through a leak conductance, and the resulting membrane voltage, tens of millivolts, is both the neuron's state and its output \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Graded chemical synapses couple these units: a depolarized presynaptic cell opens a conductance in the postsynaptic membrane whose sign makes the connection excitatory or inhibitory. The sensory channels that close the loop are the muscle afferents, Ia signaling muscle length and velocity, Ib signaling muscle force, and group II signaling length, together with heel and toe contact sensors.

The approach has been pursued most persistently by the insect-biorobotics lineage of the Quinn laboratory at Case Western Reserve University and by laboratories closely connected to it, my own included. Works in this lineage span several platforms: CPG-based neural control of a pneumatically actuated dog robot \citep{hunt_development_2017}, analytically designed dynamic neural networks for human balance control \citep{hilts_dynamic_2019}, the full-muscle rat hindlimb model and its moment-arm analysis \citep{young_analyzing_2019}, the two-layer CPG neuromechanical walker built on it \citep{deng_neuromechanical_2019}, which supplies this dissertation's controller architecture, and the Muscle Mutt quadruped, a canine-inspired BPA robot designed at my laboratory, the Agile and Adaptive Robotics Laboratory (AARL) at Portland State University, for synthetic nervous system control \citep{scharzenberger_design_2019}. Related controllers from the wider neuromechanical community include sensory-entrained CPG control of bipedal walking \citep{li_bipedal_2017}, inter-leg coordination analyses in stick-insect-inspired controllers \citep{nourse_analyzing_2019}, reinforcement-reflex hybrids in insects \citep{goldsmith_investigating_2021}, and adaptive hindlimb walking controllers \citep{schilling_adaptive_2022}.

Earlier wording or anchor Sensory feedback is not a passive correction layer but an integral part of locomotor pattern generation. Reviews of afferent control of the CPG \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998} and of muscle proprioceptive feedback and spinal networks \c… Sensory feedback is not a passive correction layer but an integral part of locomotor pattern generation. Reviews of afferent control of the CPG \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998} and of muscle proprioceptive feedback and spinal networks \citep{windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022} summarize the classical picture: group Ia afferents from muscle spindles signal muscle length and velocity, group Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs signal force, and group II afferents signal length, with load-related feedback playing a role distinct from length-related feedback during locomotion \citep{dietz_significance_2000}. Removing proprioceptive feedback degrades locomotor patterns in mice \citep{akay_degradation_2014}; proprioceptive input regulates and adapts locomotor activity \citep{lam_role_2002}; and the relative contributions of proprioceptive and vestibular systems to locomotion are the subject of ongoing study \citep{akay_relative_2021, akay_sensory_2020}. Tonic central and sensory stimuli have been shown to facilitate involuntary air-stepping in humans \citep{selionov_tonic_2009}, demonstrating that simple graded stimulation of motoneuronal and rhythmic circuits can elicit stepping-like output, an experiment readily reproduced in simulation by tonic stimulation of pattern-formation and rhythm-generator populations. The proprioceptive and contact feedback channels designed in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} follow this afferent organization.

The image is a frame from footage of a real decerebrate-cat experiment, the class of preparation on which the field's understanding of spinal locomotion has been built … Figure~\ref{fig:decerebrate_cat} shows what that accounting leaves out. The image is a frame from footage of a real decerebrate-cat experiment, the class of preparation on which the field's understanding of spinal locomotion has been built since its beginnings \citep{brown_intrinsic_1911, decerebrate_cat_footage}: a living cat, its forebrain disconnected by a brainstem transection, walks on the treadmill because the neurons distal to the laceration are still living, still connected, and still firing action potentials. The published record of this work is drawn almost exclusively in schematic, labeled boxes for half-centers and color-coded reflex arcs that are honest about the circuitry and silent about the animal. The figure is included as the counterweight, documenting what the experiments looked like, and therefore what a replacement method stands in for.

Earlier wording or anchor The experiments this research program is designed to enable, including deleting a muscle from a limb, blocking a sensory pathway, lesioning part of a rhythm generator, and applying tonic stimulation to spinal circuits, cannot be performed o… The experiments this research program is designed to enable, including deleting a muscle from a limb, blocking a sensory pathway, lesioning part of a rhythm generator, and applying tonic stimulation to spinal circuits, cannot be performed on healthy humans. Invasive intervention on the human neuromuscular system is limited to clinical populations, is tightly constrained by ethics review, and permits neither the within-subject control nor the reversibility that neuromechanical hypotheses demand. The same experiments in animals also carry real moral cost, and their justification is governed by the Three Rs framework: replacement of animal subjects with non-animal methods, reduction of the numbers required, and refinement of the remaining procedures \citep{russell_principles_1959, tannenbaum_russell_2015}. A robot that implements a validated neuromechanical hypothesis is precisely such a replacement method: every deletion, lesion, and stimulation experiment that runs on the synthetic nervous system is an experiment that does not require a living subject, and the robot population can be duplicated exactly, so that ``subjects'' are statistically identical across conditions, an experimental repeatability no breeding colony can offer. The failure modes of these experiments damage hardware, not tissue.

OpenSim supplied musculoskeletal geometry, MyoConverter translated it to MuJoCo, and SNS-Toolbox supplied neuron and synapse models \citep{delp_opensim_2007, caggiano_myosuite_2022,… Existing software supplied separate parts of the solution. OpenSim supplied musculoskeletal geometry, MyoConverter translated it to MuJoCo, and SNS-Toolbox supplied neuron and synapse models \citep{delp_opensim_2007, caggiano_myosuite_2022, todorov_mujoco_2012, nourse_sns_2023}. The MuJoCo version used here supports scripted simulation and parameter searches but uses rigid tendons; its Python interface does not provide the block-based circuit assembly needed for this workflow. Simulink supplies that graphical construction, while Simscape Multibody imports mechanical geometry, including SolidWorks-derived mechanisms. AnimatLab retains the reference controllers but is unsupported, relies on an older physics engine, and ran these simulations slowly. The tools connect these complementary environments and use matched tests to check what transfers between them.

Earlier wording or anchor A neural controller acts through the mechanics to which it is connected. Changing muscle attachments, joint motion, inertia, or actuator behavior changes the mechanical r… A neural controller acts through the mechanics to which it is connected. Changing muscle attachments, joint motion, inertia, or actuator behavior changes the mechanical response to a command and the sensory signals returned to the circuit. A controller that produces alternating motor activity can therefore fail to coordinate loading when transferred to a different body. Investigating that transfer requires tools that make the mechanical assumptions, neural computations, and exchanged signals accessible to inspection and controlled testing.

Reason and evidence The failure on ground contact matters once the reader understands what was connected and why a command can have a different mechanical consequence.

Earlier wording or anchor where $\mathbf{p}$ is the vector from the joint origin to the muscle-path crossing point and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ is the unit force direction (\texttt{MonoPamDataExplicit.m… where $\mathbf{p}$ is the vector from the joint origin to the muscle-path crossing point and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ is the unit force direction (\texttt{MonoPamDataExplicit.m} lines 156--168; identical implementations in \texttt{MonoMuscleData.m} lines 111--123, the \texttt{Mom} function of \texttt{minimizeFlxPin.m} at line 539, and \nolinkurl{MonoPam_mult.m} lines 186--201). This is the same quantity as the cross-product projection of Equation~(\ref{eq:project_ma}); the planar scalar moment arm about the joint axis is the magnitude of the in-plane components, computed as \texttt{hypot(mA(:,1), mA(:,2))} (\texttt{predictKneeFlexor20mm.m} line 217). Torque about the joint $z$-axis is $\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{f}$, evaluated only where the BPA is in tension (values are discarded for $\varepsilon < -0.02$, the excessive stretching region; \texttt{MonoPamDataExplicit.m} line 308).

Earlier wording or anchor An early experiment illustrated this problem. For a course project in ME 610: Neuromechanical Modeling, Morrow and I coupled the bipedal mechanics of \citet{li_bipedal_20… An early experiment illustrated this problem. For a course project in ME 610: Neuromechanical Modeling, Morrow and I coupled the bipedal mechanics of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} with the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. The model included bilateral thigh, shank, foot, and toe segments, sagittal-plane joints, and antagonist Hill-type muscles. I added a passive toe joint. A shared rhythm generator (RG) supplied pattern-formation (PF) and motor-neuron (MN) pathways on both sides. We adjusted currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters manually and presented the suspended result at the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. The legs cycled when suspended, but the model lost support when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}). The continued neural rhythm did not establish an effective load-bearing controller.
Proposed wording or action The joint project, individual toe, cited sources, and presentation are distinguished. For a course project in neuromechanical modeling, Morrow and I coupled the sagittal… The joint project, individual toe, cited sources, and presentation are distinguished. For a course project in neuromechanical modeling, Morrow and I coupled the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} to the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. A shared rhythm generator (RG) drove pattern-formation (PF) pathways and motor neurons (MNs) on both sides. Antagonist Hill-type muscles acted on the thighs, shanks, and feet. I added a passive toe joint. We adjusted currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand. Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Its legs cycled in suspension and the model tipped when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}).
Reason and evidence The transfer and course-project credits are useful; distinguish the joint work, the individual toe change, and the conference presentation.

Proposed wording or action The rig measures signed, synchronized torque and angular velocity and distinguishes energy delivery from absorption. Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero an… The rig measures signed, synchronized torque and angular velocity and distinguishes energy delivery from absorption. Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero angular velocity. To determine when that capacity can do work, I would measure knee torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$ on the same time base and about the same signed axis. Their product $P=\tau\omega$, in watts, is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the knee to the external load. Positive power indicates energy delivery and negative power indicates absorption. Its timing and magnitude distinguish a knee that supplies energy during extension from one that resists motion to absorb a landing load. A biomechanist can compare these phases with joint-power profiles, and a robot designer can size the actuator for both propulsion and controlled deceleration. A dynamometer on the test stand could drive flexion and extension at prescribed speeds or impose a resisting torque while the BPA moves the knee. An encoder and a joint-axis torque transducer would supply synchronized velocity and torque. Recording actuator pressure and calibrating fixture inertia, friction, and loading-connection compliance would help distinguish pneumatic delay and load--unload hysteresis from losses in the rig.
Reason and evidence State why synchronized dynamic torque and angular velocity matter, give P=τω and sign convention, and tie the dynamometer/loading proposal to delivering or absorbing power.

The stimulation recruited group~I afferents and did not isolate Ib input.

Earlier wording or anchor Excitation of the extensor MN and reciprocal inhibition of the flexor MN change the opposing moments at the knee.
Proposed wording or action A researcher can reproduce the knee experiment with \path{run_transient.m} and the archived \texttt{KneeReflexDemo} model. The driver runs the settled knee twice and adds… A researcher can reproduce the knee experiment with \path{run_transient.m} and the archived \texttt{KneeReflexDemo} model. The driver runs the settled knee twice and adds a \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{30}{\milli\second} pulse to the extensor Ia current in one run. The pulse recruited the extensor MN. The flexor was already inactive, so the rise in extensor force accounted for the initial extension (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_reflex_current}). The stimulated knee extended \ang{1.09} relative to the control, peaked \qty{111}{\milli\second} after pulse onset, and met the angle and speed recovery criteria \qty{6.355}{\second} after onset. Broader MN and Ia synaptic operating ranges allowed the model to settle before the pulse. The original narrow ranges produced sustained oscillation. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} gives the MATLAB command and the fields to inspect in the saved summary. I ran a control and a stimulated trial continuously for \qty{50}{\second} from the same initial knee flexion of \qty{0.26}{\radian}, zero angular velocity and activation, and MN voltages of \qty{-52}{\milli\volt}. Tonic drive was \qty{4.2}{\nano\ampere} to the extensor MN and \qty{2.5}{\nano\ampere} to the flexor MN. In the stimulated trial I added \qty{2}{\nano\ampere} at \path{SN_Ia_ext}, after the spindle transducer and before the extensor Ia sensory-neuron membrane, for $30.000\leq t<30.030$\,s. Angle, speed, six membrane states, and two activations settled before stimulation. I report the negative of the model's internal flexion coordinate so that positive excursions indicate extension. The baseline was the mean control angle for $25\leq t<30$\,s, \ang{-42.6392}. The initial extension came from increased extensor force, which rose from \qty{7.37}{\newton} at pulse onset to \qty{25.94}{\newton} at pulse offset. The flexor MN output was zero at baseline, and flexor force was negligible during the pulse. Flexor force subsequently exceeded \qty{0.001}{\newton} at \qty{38}{\milli\second} after onset and reached \qty{14.4}{\newton} before maximum knee extension.
Reason and evidence The measured flexor was already inactive. The corrected account attributes the initial motion to the rise in extensor force.

Earlier reviewTechnical or defense finding (77)Technical or defense finding D-01APPENDIX_D_EDITS.md · Pass through the appendix
Earlier wording or anchor 4–52, 79–81 This appendix provides the configuration details and secondary tests supporting Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}. The evidence follows the construction of a neuromechani… 4–52, 79–81 This appendix provides the configuration details and secondary tests supporting Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}. The evidence follows the construction of a neuromechanical experiment: check the mechanical model and signal interfaces, verify individual neural implementations, calibrate and test a selected controller, and examine its responses to controlled interventions. Historical comparisons are identified separately from the revised controller's current results. Neuron equations and spiking calibration remain in Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations}. \section{Mechanical-Model and Interface Verification}\label{sec:app_conversion_repairs} The conversion workflow involved two distinct problems: importing the robot's artificial-muscle routing with human muscle parameters, and repairing the converted human reference used for controller development. The first combination failed muscle-equilibrium checks because the routed lengths were incompatible with the retained human parameters. The subsequent human-model repairs described below belong to that reference-model loading path; they are not evidence that the BPA-routed model reproduces every human muscle force. \subsection{Conversion Repairs and Mechanical Checks} \paragraph{Joint directions and coordinate conventions.} Single-actuator tests exposed reversed hip-flexion and hip-adduction actions. The corresponding hinge-axis directions were negated so that the muscle actions agreed with the adopted OpenSim conventions. The knee required a different treatment: its converted flexion-negative convention was retained. Rotating the knee without updating its coupled translational coordinates gives a misleading geometry comparison, so those coordinates must follow the prescribed coupling during a pose or actuator test. These are specific joint and path checks, rather than a change from a left-handed to a right-handed model. \paragraph{Small muscles and force scales.} The quadratus femoris, gemelli, and piriformis actuators were disabled on both sides. Their six entries remain in the 92-actuator model, with no force contribution. A separate check found eight muscle-actuator entries with an active maximum-force scale of only \qty{1}{\newton}. Their active-force scales were restored from the source-model values. Table~\ref{tab:app_force_scale_repairs} lists the corrected values; each applies separately to the left and right actuator. \begin{table}[htbp] \centering \caption{Active maximum-force scales restored in the converted human model.} \label{tab:app_force_scale_repairs} \begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}} \toprule Muscle & Converted scale (\unit{\newton}) & Restored scale (\unit{\newton}) \\ \midrule Erector spinae & 1 & 2500 \\ Internal oblique & 1 & 900 \\ External oblique & 1 & 900 \\ Extensor hallucis longus & 1 & 162 \\ \bottomrule \end{tabular} \end{table} These are source-model maximum-force parameters, not measured BPA capacities or the realized force at every pose. The passive-force scales already contained the source values. The converted length ranges for these entries remain a limitation, so restoring the active scale alone does not establish full force--length agreement. \paragraph{Patella-related paths and coupled joints.} The converted moving muscle-path points use joints coupled to knee angle. Their sampled limits conflicted with the coupling constraints away from the sampled pose, producing large constraint forces and restricted motion. The coupled path-point joints were therefore left without those conflicting limits while retaining their prescribed trajectories. The anatomical driver joints were treated separately: limits were re-enabled on 14 hinges using the converted ranges. The rectus femoris route also lacked the patella tracking needed for knee-extension action; its intermediate path point was replaced by the vastus medialis patella-tracking point. The force comparison below quantifies the remaining differences at matched poses and activations. \paragraph{Contact and virtual geometry.} The converted model contained 19 explicit ground--body contact pairs, independent of geometry contact flags. Suspended tests remove these pairs; ground-contact tests retain only the six foot--ground pairs. Path-marker geometry is noncolliding. These settings isolate intended foot loading from unintended contact with other model components. These checks verify specific joint actions, coupled paths, and intended contacts. They retain the rigid-tendon approximation and do not establish full OpenSim equivalence or walking; the matched-pose force comparison below quantifies the remaining discrepancies. \subsection{Matched-Pose Force Comparison} \label{sec:muscle-models-compare} The comparison script reads OpenSim static-optimization forces and activations and assigns the corresponding poses and activations to the converted MuJoCo model. It calls the forward calculation at each pose; it does not assign the trajectory velocities or integrate muscle activation and fiber dynamics through time. OpenSim static optimization likewise solves frame-by-frame force allocation rather than a compliant-tendon forward simulation \citep{opensim_static_optimization_docs}. The comparison therefore tests force predictions along sampled poses at matched activation, not dynamic equivalence or tendon-energy storage. Table~\ref{tab:force-r2} retains the saved per-muscle statistics: $R^2=1-\mathrm{SSE}/\mathrm{SST}$, squared Pearson correlation, and the best-aligning lag in analysis frames. The calculation and saved values are in \nolinkurl{Code/MuJoCo_SNS/spinal/_muscle_force_compare.py} and \nolinkurl{muscle_force_compare.csv}. Eight of the twelve representative muscles have $R^2$ between 0.87 and 0.98 and mean-force ratios within \qty{10}{\percent}. Soleus and semimembranosus have lower agreement, and the negative $R^2$ values for rectus femoris and biceps femoris short head indicate errors larger than predicting the corresponding mean reference force. Shape correlation alone does not remove those errors. The rectus femoris path was altered during conversion, while the biceps femoris short-head result has a substantial force-scale difference. These observations identify muscles requiring closer inspection; they do not isolate routing, force-law, and velocity effects from one another. The frame-lag calculation describes alignment of these saved sequences. It cannot establish a physical delay caused by tendon compliance because the comparison does not simulate that mechanism. The results support selected pose-wise force checks, with the reported exceptions, rather than a general claim of equivalence for neural-control studies. A dynamic comparison would require matched velocities, activation histories, and explicitly specified tendon dynamics.
Proposed wording or action 4–47, 74–76 Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} describes how I connected neural controllers to musculoskeletal models. Here I document the mechanical checks, signal definitions, and i… 4–47, 74–76 Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} describes how I connected neural controllers to musculoskeletal models. Here I document the mechanical checks, signal definitions, and interventions needed to interpret their motion. A worked knee-reflex example in Section~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} can be run from the two saved Simulink models. The subsequent experiments examine timing, loading, and mechanical assistance in the coupled walkers. Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations} gives the neuron equations and spiking calibration. \section{Mechanical-Model and Interface Verification}\label{sec:app_conversion_repairs} I first applied human muscle parameters to the robot's artificial-muscle routes. The routed lengths prevented the muscles from reaching equilibrium. I therefore used the converted human reference to develop controllers and checked its joint actions, muscle forces, and contacts against their source definitions. The rerouted robot and the repaired human model have different actuator geometry. \subsection{Conversion Repairs and Mechanical Checks} \paragraph{Joint directions and coordinate conventions.} Single-actuator tests exposed reversed hip-flexion and hip-adduction actions. I reversed the corresponding hinge axes to recover the OpenSim actions and kept the converted knee coordinate, in which flexion is negative. At each knee angle I also applied its prescribed translations. Rotating the knee while holding those coordinates fixed changes the muscle paths and invalidates the pose comparison. \paragraph{Small muscles and force scales.} I disabled quadratus femoris, gemelli, and piriformis bilaterally. Their six entries remain in the 92-actuator model with zero force. Eight other muscle entries had an active maximum-force scale of only \qty{1}{\newton}. I restored the four bilateral scales from the source model (Table~\ref{tab:app_force_scale_repairs}). \begin{table}[htbp] \centering \caption{Active maximum-force scales restored in the converted human model.} \label{tab:app_force_scale_repairs} \begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}} \toprule Muscle & Converted scale (\unit{\newton}) & Restored scale (\unit{\newton}) \\ \midrule Erector spinae & 1 & 2500 \\ Internal oblique & 1 & 900 \\ External oblique & 1 & 900 \\ Extensor hallucis longus & 1 & 162 \\ \bottomrule \end{tabular} \end{table} The passive-force scales already matched the source. The converted length ranges still differ, so the restored maximum forces alone cannot predict force agreement at a given pose. \paragraph{Patella-related paths and coupled joints.} The converted moving path points follow knee angle through coupled joints. Their sampled limits conflicted with the prescribed trajectories away from the sampled pose, restricting motion and producing large constraint forces. I removed the conflicting limits from the path-point joints, kept their couplings, and restored the converted ranges on 14 anatomical hinges. For rectus femoris I substituted the patella-tracking point of vastus medialis for the intermediate point that had failed to track the patella during knee extension. \paragraph{Contact and virtual geometry.} The converted model defined 19 explicit ground--body contact pairs independently of its geometry contact flags. I removed all 19 for suspended tests and retained the six foot--ground pairs for ground tests. Path-marker geometry was noncolliding. These choices determine which bodies can load a foot or supply external support during a trial. \subsection{Matched-Pose Force Comparison} \label{sec:muscle-models-compare} At each reference pose I assigned the OpenSim static-optimization activations and coordinates to the converted MuJoCo model and evaluated its muscle forces. OpenSim static optimization allocates forces frame by frame \citep{opensim_static_optimization_docs}. Neither the trajectory velocities nor a forward history of activation or fiber state entered this comparison. It measures agreement at matched posture and activation under the converted rigid-tendon approximation. Table~\ref{tab:force-r2} gives $R^2=1-\mathrm{SSE}/\mathrm{SST}$, squared Pearson correlation, and the lag in analysis frames that best aligns each pair of force sequences. The calculation and its per-muscle results are in \nolinkurl{Code/MuJoCo_SNS/spinal/_muscle_force_compare.py} and \nolinkurl{muscle_force_compare.csv}. Eight of twelve right-side muscles had $R^2$ between 0.87 and 0.98 and mean MuJoCo forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of OpenSim. Mean MuJoCo/OpenSim force ratios for the other four were 0.916 for soleus, 0.776 for semimembranosus, 1.088 for rectus femoris, and 1.846 for biceps femoris short head. The latter two had negative $R^2$, so predicting the mean reference force would give a smaller squared error. For biceps femoris short head, a squared shape correlation of 0.868 concealed its large force-scale error. The altered rectus femoris path is one candidate explanation for its discrepancy. Lag describes alignment of the sampled force sequences. Attributing a lag or scale error to a particular mechanism would require matched velocities, activation histories, and tendon dynamics. The comparison preserves the per-muscle statistics. The historical framewise MuJoCo forces are unavailable for a fresh calculation of every $R^2$.

Earlier wording or anchor 84–115 \subsection{Neural and Actuator Signal Contracts}\label{sec:app_signal_contracts} The graphical and programmatic implementations require the same represented qua… 84–115 \subsection{Neural and Actuator Signal Contracts}\label{sec:app_signal_contracts} The graphical and programmatic implementations require the same represented quantities, units, signs, and update order at their interfaces. Neural membrane voltages, applied currents, and conductances use millivolts, nanoamperes, and microsiemens, respectively. The neuronal equations and spiking calibration are given in Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations}. The one-input SNS-Simscape synapse transmits the pair $[g_k,\,g_kE_k]^{\mathsf T}$ to its postsynaptic neuron, which evaluates \begin{equation} I_{\mathrm{syn}}=\sum_k g_kE_k-V\sum_k g_k =\sum_k g_k(E_k-V). \label{eq:app_synaptic_contract} \end{equation} Here $g_k$ is the conductance calculated from the presynaptic voltage and the specified saturation ramp, and $E_k$ is the reversal potential. Summing these two transmitted quantities within the neuron preserves the conductance-based driving force without a separate postsynaptic-voltage wire to every synapse. The \texttt{SynSum} block combines additional incoming pairs using the same operation. Motor output, actuator force, and sensory return remain separate interfaces. The biological-muscle block accepts dimensionless activation, musculotendon length in metres, and shortening velocity in metres per second. The characterized BPA blocks accept pressure in kilopascals and path length in metres and return tensile force in newtons. Their mask parameters specify resting, tendon, and fitting lengths. The quasi-static pressure--length force calculation does not supply valve-flow or pressure-transient dynamics. Conversely, the reduced knee demonstration uses its declared simplified actuator law and is not an additional validation of the characterized BPA equations. The MuJoCo--Simulink bridge exchanges command and measurement arrays between an existing MuJoCo mechanism and a Simulink controller. Each experiment must retain its array ordering, joint sign convention, command scaling, and timestep with its recording. This runtime interface does not translate arbitrary Simscape mechanisms into MuJoCo. The conversion records also identify machine-specific geometry paths and external-source patches that require preflight checking before a fresh MyoConverter run; the demonstrated repaired models are not evidence of a universal one-step conversion process. \section{Implementation and Circuit-Response Checks}\label{sec:sns_ports}\label{sec:crossengine_methods} Implementation agreement is assessed with a common circuit specification, identical input samples, and matched update settings. A separate coupled-model test is needed to establish what those neural outputs do to a mechanical model. This distinction also prevents a successful small circuit from conferring verification on a larger controller. \subsection{Matched Rhythm-Core Implementations} The contact-driven W2L comparison maps corresponding neuron parameters and shared rhythm pathways from the 95-neuron NumPy network into a representative 26-neuron Simulink core. Drive and prescribed heel inputs match. Over the post-startup \qtyrange{2}{12}{\second} interval, burst periods matched at \qty{1.000}{\second} and all ten expected bursts were reproduced. The correlation comparison uses 5,000 matching \qty{2}{\milli\second} samples through \qty{11.998}{\second}; best-lag correlations of the four RG traces were at least 0.99996 at a \qty{2}{\milli\second} relative lag (Figure~\ref{fig:w2l_crossengine}). Removing the phasic heel inputs caused latching in both implementations. The shared-signal agreement does not establish identical complete networks, autonomous oscillation, or sample-exact transfer. \begin{figure}[p] \centering \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.55\textheight,keepaspectratio]{w2l_crossengine_20261116.png} \caption[Matched-input W2L rhythm-core comparison]{Corresponding W2L rhythm signals in the full NumPy network and representative Simulink core under identical drive and prescribed heel inputs. The reported correlation is a best-lag measure with \qty{2}{\milli\second} relative alignment; it is not unshifted sample agreement or a comparison of independent closed-loop mechanical trajectories.} \label{fig:w2l_crossengine} \end{figure} The separately translated Deng circuit produced a \qty{1.938}{\second} period against a \qty{1.94}{\second} NumPy reference, with antagonist correlation $r=-0.86$. Its archived AnimatLab configuration had an approximately \qty{0.221}{\second} period and an in-phase bilateral rhythm. The parameterizations differ, so antagonist alternation alone does not establish quantitative equivalence. A full 410-neuron export agreed with its NumPy reference to \qty{4.2e-06}{\milli\volt} over the early transient and subsequently diverged. A separate constant-drive realization approached a fixed point while its reference oscillated. These outcomes require configuration-specific verification before parameter transfer.
Proposed wording or action 78–113 \subsection{Neural and Actuator Signal Contracts}\label{sec:app_signal_contracts} Membrane voltage, current, and conductance are represented in millivolts, nanoa… 78–113 \subsection{Neural and Actuator Signal Contracts}\label{sec:app_signal_contracts} Membrane voltage, current, and conductance are represented in millivolts, nanoamperes, and microsiemens in both the graphical and programmatic implementations. The one-input SNS-Simscape synapse passes the pair $[g_k,\,g_kE_k]^{\mathsf T}$ to the postsynaptic neuron, which calculates \begin{equation} I_{\mathrm{syn}}=\sum_k g_kE_k-V\sum_k g_k =\sum_k g_k(E_k-V). \label{eq:app_synaptic_contract} \end{equation} Here $g_k$ is the conductance calculated from the presynaptic voltage and the specified saturation ramp, and $E_k$ is the reversal potential. Summing these two transmitted quantities within the neuron preserves the conductance-based driving force without a separate postsynaptic-voltage wire to every synapse. The \texttt{SynSum} block combines additional incoming pairs using the same operation. The biological-muscle block takes dimensionless activation, musculotendon length in metres, and shortening velocity in metres per second. The characterized BPA blocks take pressure in kilopascals and path length in metres and return tensile force in newtons. Their mask parameters specify resting, tendon, and fitting lengths. The pressure--length law describes quasi-static force. Valve flow and pressure transients require separate models. The reduced knee and loaded-cup demonstrations each implement six connections. On each side, Ia excites its own MN and inhibits the antagonist MN, and Ib inhibits its own MN. The Ia block combines a position signal and signed velocity and clips its output to \qtyrange{0}{10}{\nano\ampere}. For knee angle $q$ and angular range $R$, the extensor velocity input is $\dot q/R$. The implemented flexor path applies a second gain of $-1/R$ to that signal, giving $-\dot q/R^2$. In the cup model, the two muscles receive opposite signed deviations and velocities, each divided by \qty{0.3}{\radian}. Both models feed tensile force directly to Ib. The knee's extensor and flexor gains are 0.0200 and \qty{0.0222}{\nano\ampere\per\newton}, respectively. Both cup gains are \qty{0.008}{\nano\ampere\per\newton}. The knee uses a simplified linear actuator. In the cup, filtered activation $A$ supplies $620A$\,kPa to each characterized BPA20 block. Neither circuit has an independent group II or foot-contact input. The graphical editor's Build action imports the saved graded neurons, synapses, and external current destinations into Simulink. In the saved W2L example, the left extensor PF projects to the left extensor MN, and the corresponding left flexor PF projects to the flexor MN. A user can inspect each connection's conductance, reversal potential, and activation ramp. The separate demonstration builders add mechanical equations, actuator blocks, and sensory wiring. The worked knee experiment below uses the coupled model generated by its demonstration builder. The MathWorks MuJoCo--Simulink C++ S-function exchanges command and measurement arrays with an existing MuJoCo mechanism. I adapted the build for MuJoCo 2.3.7 and Windows MinGW, selected keyframe 0 on reset when present, and added five right-side readbacks to an MJCF copy. They report knee angle and angular speed and vastus medialis path length, velocity, and force. The runtime interface preserves the mechanism supplied to it. Preparing that mechanism from OpenSim requires the corresponding geometry paths and MyoConverter patches. The E1 demonstration sends the right vastus medialis measurements through Ia, II, and Ib and returns a command to that actuator. Its length encoder computes $\operatorname{clip}\!\left(0.5+L/[2(L_{\max}-L_0)],0,1\right)$ from raw path length $L$, with $L_0=\qty{0.1734624224}{\meter}$ and $L_{\max}=\qty{0.24673}{\meter}$. The encoder reached 1 at all 300 noninitial \qty{5}{\milli\second} samples in each feedback-on and feedback-off recording. The II block therefore returned a constant \qty{4}{\nano\ampere}, and the length contribution to Ia stayed constant. The velocity and force signals could still vary. E1 demonstrates bidirectional command and measurement exchange. A length-evoked response would require an encoder with a changing output over the measured range. \section{Implementation and Circuit-Response Checks}\label{sec:sns_ports}\label{sec:crossengine_methods} I compared neural implementations with a common circuit definition, prescribed input samples, and matched update settings. Coupled experiments then tested the action of those outputs through a specified mechanical model. \subsection{Matched Rhythm-Core Implementations} I mapped the shared rhythm pathways of the 95-neuron NumPy W2L network into a 26-neuron Simulink core and prescribed the same drive and heel inputs. Best-lag correlation aligns the signals by \qty{2}{\milli\second}. Each implementation received the same external input sequence.} \label{fig:w2l_crossengine} \end{figure} The separately translated Deng circuit produced a \qty{1.938}{\second} period against a \qty{1.94}{\second} NumPy reference, with antagonist correlation $r=-0.86$. Its archived AnimatLab configuration had an approximately \qty{0.221}{\second} period and an in-phase bilateral rhythm. The parameterizations differ, so antagonist alternation alone does not establish quantitative equivalence. A full 410-neuron export agreed with its NumPy reference to \qty{4.2e-06}{\milli\volt} over the early transient and subsequently diverged. A separate constant-drive realization approached a fixed point while its reference oscillated. These outcomes require configuration-specific verification before parameter transfer.

Angle, speed, six membrane states, and two activations settled before stimulation. I report the negative of the model's internal flexion coordinate so that positive excursions indicate extension. The baseline was the mean control angle for $25\leq t<30$\,s, \ang{-42.6392}. The initial extension came from increased extensor force, which rose from \qty{7.37}{\newton} at pulse onset to \qty{25.94}{\newton} at pulse offset. The flexor MN output was zero at baseline, and flexor force was negligible during the pulse. The stimulated knee reached \ang{1.0908} more extension than the concurrent control \qty{111}{\milli\second} after pulse onset.
